extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in entertainment, the Oscars, and Conan O’Brien
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for preparing to host a major televised awards show (the Oscars), emphasizing comedic craft, preparation, and tone. Focuses on what the host did and valued while preparing rather than a formal checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose challenging/daunting gigs
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am drawn to the things that scare me.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing a hosting gig as a challenge/‘thankless gig’ can be part of its appeal; taking on scary or high-pressure jobs is a deliberate career choice and creative provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain genuine excitement, not cynicism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Conan O’Brien is not a cynic — at least not when it comes to the Oscars... he is genuinely excited — ‘I get to do this!’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach the event with authentic enthusiasm rather than ironic detachment; audience perception of the host’s sincerity matters for tone and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek an approach that preserves creative happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: “What’s the best way to tackle this? How? In a way that makes me creatively happy?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal creative satisfaction as a criterion for choices about material and presentation — the host should aim for an approach that aligns with their artistic standards, not just perceived external expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble a trusted writing team
rubrics_metrics.description: “His preparation has included bringing in 10 of his own writers to work with Oscar-night stalwarts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine your own writers with established show veterans; bringing a core team you trust is a concrete preparation step to shape the material and voice for the broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with veteran/stalwart staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with “Oscar-night stalwarts” alongside personal writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance new or personal collaborators with institutional expertise—working with long-time staff helps align comedy to the specific rhythms and expectations of a long-running awards show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test material live and with close reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: He’s been “running jokes by the crew, and dropping in at clubs in Los Angeles to try out material.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try jokes on multiple audiences and trusted colleagues before the broadcast; use club runs and crew feedback to gauge timing, punchlines, and audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on iterative testing rather than formula
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no formula. ‘It’s frustrating, but it’s not math. You can’t prove it. The only way to find out is to try it on people.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept uncertainty in what will land; iteratively refine material through real-world testing rather than attempting to apply a fixed recipe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate personal authenticity and anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal elements inform preparation — e.g., after family loss and evacuation he kept a meaningful E.B. White letter visible while preparing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on personal experiences or tangible anchors can ground the host emotionally and inform authentic material or tone for the performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use live-performance instincts developed over time
rubrics_metrics.description: “I started seriously writing comedy around the time I was 18... and it’s what I think about all the time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on long-cultivated instincts and craft; years of writing and stage work inform judgment about material and delivery during high-stakes hosting.
